analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal tax breaks for oil and gas companies and raises their taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill to end oil and gas tax subsidies was introduced in January 2025 and has sat in the House Ways and Means Committee ever since, with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill takes away a list of special tax deductions and credits that oil and gas companies get but other businesses mostly do not — including write-offs for drilling costs, tax credits for marginal wells and enhanced oil recovery, and a depreciation rule that lets producers shelter income. It also blocks the largest oil companies from a favorable accounting method and extends the federal excise tax on imported oil to tar sands and oil shale products. The money these rules currently let companies keep would flow to the Treasury instead.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, because the special tax breaks repealed by this bill would no longer reduce federal revenue. The bill also funds oil spill cleanup more fully by taxing imported tar sands oil, which currently escapes the tax that pays for it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers and oil spill cleanup funds

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the tax credit for producing oil from marginal wells, the enhanced oil recovery credit, the deduction for intangible drilling costs, percentage depletion, and the deduction for tertiary injectants — all targeted breaks for oil and gas producers [S2]

Excludes oil and gas production, refining, and distribution income from the pass-through business tax deduction, and blocks major integrated oil companies from using LIFO accounting, which currently reduces their reported taxable income [S2]

Expands the definition of taxable imported crude oil to include tar sands and oil shale products, and lets the Treasury add other petroleum products to the excise tax that funds oil spill response [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, from small independent producers of marginal wells to the largest integrated oil majors, would pay more in taxes. Some of that cost could be passed to consumers at the pump, and small operators who rely on the marginal well credit and percentage depletion would face the largest proportional hit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies, especially small producers

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the marginal well credit and percentage depletion, which are used heavily by small independent producers andstripper-well operators rather than the big majors; ending them could hasten the shutdown and abandonment of marginal wells [S2]

Repealing drilling tax breaks raises production costs; some portion of that would likely be passed through to consumers in the form of higher fuel prices, and domestic producers argue the breaks offset higher costs than foreign state-owned rivals face [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: closing industry-specific tax loopholes raises revenue from a profitable sector and stops the tax code from favoring one industry. The main honest cost is that some relief flows to small producers, not just majors, and energy prices could tick up as costs are passed through. On balance the bill's targets are well-defined tax preferences, though its fate suggests the committee with jurisdiction has no interest in advancing it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since.

narrative.text: Introduced on January 14, 2025, by Rep. Sean Casten with 11 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3]
Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction; the complete action history shows no further action [S5]
The bill would repeal or limit a series of tax deductions and credits specific to oil and gas production [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies keep their tax breaks, since the bill has not moved in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies keep their tax breaks

for.name: Rep. Sean Casten
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Oil and Gas Tax Subsidies Act of 2025 in the House

for.name: 16 Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. Beyer, Levin, Khanna, Schakowsky, and others
for.what_they_did: Cosigned the bill; every cosponsor is a Democrat

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 14, 2025, and has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — in the year and a half since

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Largest beneficiary of the tax breaks the bill repeals
against.what_they_did: The industry has long defended these tax provisions, including marginal well credits, percentage depletion, and intangible drilling cost deductions, through lobbying and campaign support for opponents

sides.party_line_note: All 12 original sponsors and all 16 cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill sits in a committee whose Republican majority has not scheduled it for any action [S3][S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill repeals their industry-specific deductions and credits — intangible drilling costs, percentage depletion, the marginal well and enhanced oil recovery credits — costing the sector billions in tax benefits that ordinary taxpayers would otherwise effectively underwrite [S2].
Large integrated producers (500,000+ barrels per day) would lose LIFO accounting, which defers taxes, and would be barred from the pass-through deduction on oil and gas income [S2].
The marginal well credit and percentage depletion are concentrated among small producers of low-output wells; repeal bears on them proportionally hardest and could accelerate well shutdowns [S2].

industries.industry: Importers of tar sands and oil shale products
industries.note: The bill extends the petroleum excise tax that funds oil spill cleanup to imported bitumen, tar sands, and oil shale oils that currently escape it [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the House majority and the Ways and Means chairmanship, a bill with no Republican support that has been idle since January 2025 is very likely to die quietly in committee without a hearing or vote.
